# The Best Liar of All {#the-best-liar-of-all}

The strangest thing is that the most persuasive voice in all this is your own.

Men in the trap aren't weak-willed. It takes real stamina to keep up a secret for twenty years. The trouble is where the strength goes. We pour it into defending the habit. Then, when we try to quit and fail, we turn it on ourselves. Failing at something is one thing. Hating yourself for it is another, and it leaks out into everything else. You stop going to the gym. The diet lasts until Thursday. Your children get the worst of your temper.

Nobody argues with himself about whether to give up golf. With this we argue every night, and we think that's normal.

So from now on, treat everything you've been told about this habit the way you'd treat a pushy salesman. Smile and nod, and don't sign. That goes for "you need it" and for "it's who you are". It also goes for the idea of a safe version. "Only in the shower", "only without a screen" and "only on weekends" were all invented by the Little Monster. Keep asking yourself two questions. "Why am I doing this? Do I actually need to?"

Of course you don't.

Once you're in the trap, the lies get help from inside. Some part of you knows the Little Monster expects feeding, and it will defend his dinner against any argument. That's fear: the fear of that empty, fidgety feeling.

The trap closes slowly. Most men don't know they're in it until the day they try to leave, and even then plenty won't admit it. Anyone who has raised the subject with a young man knows how the conversation goes:

"You know the only reason you keep doing it is that you can't stop?"

"Nonsense. I like it. If I didn't, I'd stop."

"Then stop for a month, just to show me."

"Why would I? I like it."

"Stop for a month to show yourself."

"There's no point. I told you, I like it."

He likes it so much that he won't risk finding out.

## "Giving up" {-}

One more thing keeps the lies standing. We never question them. We believe what we've always heard, most of all from the people we trust.

The world says the man who stops is missing out. So be clear about who is missing out. It isn't the man who stopped. It's the man who carries on. He hands over his energy, his time, his confidence and his peace of mind. And what does he get for it?

Nothing.

Each time, he gets the brief illusion of returning to the calm that the free man has all day long.

The phrase "giving up" is the plainest example of the lie. It smuggles in the idea of a sacrifice. But there's nothing to give up. You'll be getting rid of a parasite and gaining a great deal. So we'll drop that phrase here and now. In this book you don't "give up" lust. You stop. You quit. Best of all, **YOU ESCAPE.**

The world's lies are general. Your own are specific: this habit helps me with *this*, at *these* times.

So let's go through your day and find them.
